newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S. Africa's Inkatha rejoins constitutional talks.
newsitem.headline: S. Africa's Inkatha rejoins constitutional talks.

text.p: South Africa's Zulu-based Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP) ended an 18-month boycott of the country's constitution-writing process on Tuesday, but political sources said it was unlikely to stay for long.

IFP negotiator Peter Smith became the first Inkatha member to participate in constitutional talks since February last year, offering an apology but no explanation for being an hour late for a meeting on provincial and municipal powers.

The IFP, headed by conservative Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi, decided to rejoin the constitutional process after talks last week with the ruling African National Congress (ANC) and the white-led National Party (NP).

Senior ANC and NP negotiators said privately, however, they had little hope of a final settlement including Inkatha, whose demand for a federalist model of post-apartheid government differs greatly from the largely centrist constitution.
One party strategist said he feared the IFP would haggle and obstruct until the ANC was forced to declare a stalemate and use its majority to ensure passage of a new constitution.

"It's all about who should take the blame for Inkatha's opposition to the new constitution. At the moment the situation is that they walked out. Buthelezi would rather have the record show that they were forced out," he said.
Pointing to Buthelezi's reputation for brinkmanship, Democratic Party negotiator James Selfe commented: "I think there could be an element of gamesmanship here, too."

Buthelezi's party, which seeks to swing power from the central government towards provincial administrations, won 10 percent of the 20 million votes cast in South Africa's first democratic elections in April 1994, mostly in KwaZulu-Natal.
Inkatha quit the constitution-writing assembly in February 1995 when the ANC reneged on a pre-election promise to submit differences with the IFP to international mediation.
The IFP was the only party to boycott a May meeting at which the 490-member Constitutional Assembly adopted a draft constitution with only two votes against.
Selfe said it was important to bring Inkatha's conservative Zulu members on board, adding: "Otherwise their constituency will continue to be a festering sore. Its a big constituency."

The top-ranking Constitutional Court praised the draft, but referred it back for more work on eight issues, which gave Inkatha an opportunity to return and influence the final text on its bottomline issues: Provincial and municipal powers.
Smith declined an invitation by committee chairman Pravin Gordhan of the ANC on Tuesday to explain the decision to end the boycott or to make an opening statement.
His only comment was that Inkatha would interpret the mandate for renegotiation given by the court more broadly than the ANC, which wants to make as few changes as possible.
The CA, comprising the national assembly and senate sitting together, has until Friday next week to adopt amendments if the text is to be approved before the court's Christmas recess.
Gordhan said he was confidant that the seven parties in the CA could meet the October 11 deadline, adding: "I believe we can do it in 24 hours if there is a political will to do so."
Selfe called the deadline artificial, adding: "If we have to work through our recess, I fail to see why the justices shouldn't work through theirs."
